indications: Degenerative spondylolisthesis with stenosis where instability, slip progression or back pain is a significant part of the problem, after individual discussion (NASS and AANS/CNS guidelines; trial evidence on adding fusion is conflicting).
Isthmic spondylolisthesis with radicular symptoms or disabling pain after failed non-operative treatment.
Recurrent disc herniation with instability, or a decompression that will remove enough facet or pars to destabilise the segment.
Selected deformity, trauma, tumour or infection, where the principles are the same but the plan differs.
contraindications: Low back pain alone: NICE NG59 advises not to offer spinal fusion for low back pain except as part of a randomised controlled trial.
Active infection at the operative site, unless fusion is the treatment for the infection.
Severe osteoporosis without a plan to augment fixation.
Uncontrolled medical comorbidity; smoking increases non-union and should be addressed before elective fusion.
Psychosocial factors that predict a poor outcome, addressed before surgery.
preparation: MRI and standing radiographs, with flexion and extension views, to show the slip and its mobility; CT for pedicle size and trajectory, or for navigation.
Bone health assessment in older patients and smokers.
Record the neurological examination and the Oswestry Disability Index.
Blood: group and cross-match per local blood loss risk; consider cell salvage and tranexamic acid per anaesthetic protocol.

Consent should include nerve root injury and new leg pain or weakness from a misplaced screw or cage, dural tear, infection, blood loss and transfusion, non-union, implant failure or loosening, adjacent segment degeneration, failure to relieve back pain, venous thromboembolism, perioperative visual loss, and wrong level.
positioning: Prone on a radiolucent frame that leaves the abdomen free and maintains lumbar lordosis; hips extended.
Eyes free of pressure, checked at intervals and recorded.
Image intensifier or navigation set up so that true AP and lateral views of each pedicle can be obtained before preparing.
equipment: Image intensifier or navigation; neurophysiological monitoring with triggered EMG if used.
Pedicle screw system with rods, cages, trials and graft material.
Pedicle awl, probe, ball-tipped feeler, taps.
High-speed drill, osteotomes, Kerrison rongeurs, disc shavers and curettes.
Microscope or loupes and headlight; cell salvage.
anatomy: The lumbar pedicle entry point is at the junction of the transverse process and the lateral edge of the superior articular process, at the base of the pars. Pedicles converge medially and their angulation increases from L1 to L5.
The medial and inferior pedicle walls lie against the traversing and exiting roots; a medial or inferior breach is the dangerous one.

In a TLIF, removing the inferior articular process of the upper vertebra and the superior articular process of the lower vertebra opens Kambin triangle: the exiting root above, the traversing root and dura medially, and the pedicle below.
The great vessels and the common iliac vessels lie directly in front of the lower lumbar discs; an anterior breach of the vertebral body or the annulus can injure them.
criticalSafety: Image or navigate every pedicle before a screw is inserted, and probe all four walls and the floor.
Know where the exiting root is before working in the foramen: it lies just under the pedicle above.
Never pass a disc instrument through the anterior annulus; check depth on the lateral image.
An unexplained drop in blood pressure during a discectomy is a great vessel injury until proved otherwise: pack, turn supine and call for a vascular surgeon.
structuresAtRisk: Great vessels and iliac vessels anterior to the spine
Pedicle walls and the adjacent facet joint above the fusion
Eyes and pressure areas in long prone surgery
commonErrors: Medial pedicle breach from a too-medial entry or too-converging trajectory.
Violating the facet joint above the fusion with the top screws.
Retracting the dura or the traversing root to insert the cage instead of removing more facet.
Fusing in reduced lordosis because of positioning.
complications: Root injury and new radicular pain or weakness from a misplaced screw or cage.
Major haemorrhage, including great vessel injury.
Deep infection, which may need debridement with retention of implants.
Non-union, screw loosening, cage subsidence or migration.
postop: Neurological observations of leg power and sensation against the baseline; new weakness or radicular pain needs imaging of screw and cage position.
Analgesia per enhanced recovery protocol, early mobilisation and physiotherapy.
Thromboprophylaxis per NICE NG89 and local timing after spinal surgery.
Standing radiographs before discharge or at follow-up per local practice.
Smoking cessation and bone health follow-up; outcome scores at follow-up.

steps.emphasis: Be explicit that fusion is for leg symptoms and instability, and that relief of back pain is not assured.
Read the level and the side of the TLIF from the MRI aloud; record leg power and the Oswestry score.
State the levels, the side for the interbody approach, blood availability, cell salvage and monitoring.
Redose the antibiotic for a long operation or heavy blood loss.
Hips extended on the frame to keep lordosis; the segment is fused in the position it lies in.
Triggered EMG for screws and free-running EMG for the TLIF corridor, if monitoring is used.
Count from the sacrum; confirm the level again with markers in the pedicles.
Expose to the tips of the transverse processes at the fused levels only, preserving the facet capsule above.
Confirm screw diameters and lengths from the CT measurements before opening.
Decompress as the stenosis requires; the TLIF side is decompressed through the facetectomy.
Through Kambin triangle, without retracting the dura beyond the medial edge of the pedicle.
Distract on the opposite screws, insert the cage obliquely or across the midline, then release distraction.
After a cage or a screw: check the implant first.
Root-by-root leg power and sensation, with new radicular pain as a trigger for imaging.
Record screw and cage details, the side of the TLIF, monitoring events and the images saved.

step.tlif.pedicle-screws.title: Pedicle screw insertion
step.tlif.pedicle-screws.why: The pedicle is a narrow bony tube with a nerve root on its medial and inferior sides. A screw that breaches medially or inferiorly can injure a root; one that breaches anteriorly can reach the great vessels. Each step from entry to screw is a chance to detect a wrong trajectory before it becomes a screw.
how: Identify the entry point at the junction of the transverse process and the lateral superior articular process, and decorticate it with a burr.
Advance the pedicle probe with gentle, steady pressure along the planned convergence and the angle of the endplate, without forcing it; a sudden give suggests a breach.
Feel the floor and all four walls with a ball-tipped feeler, and measure the depth.
Confirm position on AP and lateral images or navigation; test with triggered EMG if available, interpreting thresholds with the neurophysiologist.
Tap if the system requires it, re-feel the tract, then insert the screw of the planned diameter and length. Image again.
structuresAtRisk: Great vessels anterior to the vertebral body
pitfalls: Forcing the probe when it meets resistance.
Skipping the feeler check because the image looked acceptable.
A screw so long that it breaches the anterior cortex.

step.tlif.facetectomy.title: Unilateral facetectomy and opening Kambin triangle
step.tlif.facetectomy.why: A full facetectomy creates the corridor for the cage without having to retract the dura or the traversing root. The exiting root lies just under the pedicle above and is injured when the surgeon works too high or too lateral in the foramen.
how: On the side of the worse leg symptoms, osteotomise the inferior articular process of the upper vertebra and remove it; keep it as autograft.
Remove the superior articular process of the lower vertebra flush with the pedicle below.
Remove the ligamentum flavum to expose the lateral dura and the traversing root.
Identify the exiting root in the upper part of the foramen and protect it; coagulate the foraminal veins with bipolar diathermy.
Confirm the disc space between the exiting root above, the traversing root medially and the pedicle below.
pitfalls: Working too high in the foramen and injuring the exiting root or its dorsal root ganglion.
Leaving too much superior articular process, then retracting the dura to gain access.

step.tlif.rods.title: Rods, compression and posterolateral graft
step.tlif.rods.why: Rods connect the screws into a construct. Compression across the cage restores lordosis and loads the graft, but compression also narrows the foramen, which must be checked afterwards.
how: Decorticate the transverse processes and facet remnants on the side without the TLIF, and lay autograft or graft material for a posterolateral fusion if planned.
Cut and contour the rods to the lordosis wanted; seat them in the screw heads without forcing a screw to pull out of its pedicle.
Compress across the cage to restore lordosis, then tighten the set screws to the system's torque.
Check the foramina on the TLIF side after compression with a probe, and take final AP and lateral images of the whole construct.
structuresAtRisk: Exiting roots in the foramen (narrowed by compression)
pitfalls: Forcing a misaligned rod into a screw head.
Compressing without a cage in place, narrowing the foramen.
